title: Record super raid for dental work leaves hole in retirement savings
full_text:
A surge in people tapping their superannuation to pay for new teeth and other dental bills is eroding retirement savings, with financial advisers and dentists warning some savers are using the early-release scheme to seek cosmetic services or offshore procedures that could deliver a holiday on the side.
New figures from the Australian Taxation Office show super fund members withdrew $892m early from their nest eggs last financial year to cover dental treatments, a massive 421 per cent surge since 2021-22.
Dentist bills have, by far, been the fastest-growing category of superannuation early release claims, amid concerns about third-party spruikers helping people dip into their super for cosmetic dentistry, and financial advisers warn the final cost to savers can be more than 10 times their initial withdrawal.
The latest figures show dental claims represented a majority of payouts approved for compassionate release of super in 2025-26, and the 33,550 dental patients approved comprised more than half of the overall 60,600 approvals.
The ATO has been cracking down on early super rorts, working with health practitioner regulators to target misconduct and “take strong action against third-party facilitators”.
Last week the ATO and Australian Federal Police raided a Melbourne dental practice linked to a former health practitioner, who it is alleged supplied fraudulent medical reports and, using recruiters, supported 1178 compassionate release applications that saw $36.4m withdrawn from super.
“This wasn’t a misunderstanding of the rules,” ATO acting deputy commissioner Pennie Snowden said. “These allegations point to a deliberate attempt to take advantage of a system designed to help Australians in genuine need.”
While growth in early-release approvals for dental treatment has slowed in the past 12 months, more than $2.7bn has been approved in the past five financial years. The average amount approved is more than $26,500, suggesting that more people are opting for expensive implants – where a full upper or lower set can cost between $15,000 and $50,000, rather than traditional dentures that can cost between $2500 and $7000.
The ATO does not keep age-based data specifically related to dental treatment, but says for overall compassionate release of super approvals, 77 per cent come from people aged between 31 and 55.
Compassionate early release of superannuation
Freshwater Wealth partner Roger Perrett said a 30-year-old withdrawing $26,000 from their super could reduce their eventual retirement savings by almost $327,000, while for a 40-year-old the estimate was $158,500 and a 50-year-old could miss out on $76,900, based on average annual investment returns.
“Australians should understand the long-term opportunity cost of withdrawing retirement savings, particularly younger people who could sacrifice decades of compound investment growth,” Mr Perrett said.
“Accessing superannuation for necessary medical treatment may be appropriate, but it should be a last resort after considering other funding options,” he said.
In some cases, people are withdrawing their super then heading overseas for cheaper dental work in countries including Vietnam, which is aggressively targeting medical tourism.
Australian Dental Association president Chris Sanzaro said the risks of doing this included lower standards overseas, unlicensed operators, being forced to spend more when offshore and difficulties if something went wrong.
“Anecdotally, we have heard reports of people getting their quote done, getting their money released from super for Australian prices then going overseas and getting it done cheaper, and using the money elsewhere in their life,” Dr Sanzaro said.
“Certainly there’s some operators operating outside the rules – some dentists and also some third parties.
“Cosmetic improvements fall outside the scope of the legislation unless someone is in pain already and the cosmetic improvements happen as part of the treatment.”
Dr Sanzaro said factors driving the surge in using super for dental costs included an increased awareness of being able to access super, cost-of-living stresses and social pressure to have perfect-looking teeth.
“When the government allowed people to dip into their super to meet their living costs because of the Covid lockdowns, everyone started looking at the legislation and some thought ‘hang on a second, there’s this whole thing in there about compassionate release that we have never really used that much before’,” he said.
“There’s a societal change too. There’s been a generation that’s gone through and accepted ending up with full dentures, and there’s a group going through now going, ‘I don’t think I want to end up with removable dentures – that’s grandma and grandpa’ … and therefore they’re going through more expensive treatments like maintaining teeth and implants.”
The Super Members Council wants a ban on predatory advertising that encourages people to withdraw super for non-essential dental and medical services.
“ Compassionate release is an important safety net, but it must always have very strong safeguards to protect Australians’ retirement savings,” council chief executive Misha Schubert said.
“It should never be able to be used as a sales tactic or a business model.
“Parliament should urgently ban predatory ads that promote early withdrawal of super for non-essential treatments and stop third parties from taking a cut of your super to fill out the forms.”
Dr Sanzaro said the federal government needed to improve access to publicly funded dental services.
“We’re still missing a national oral health plan,” he said. “We were it promised it in 2024 and it’s now 2026.”
